body.body: AIStore **5.1** is a short-cycle reliability and scalability release following the major [5.0](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/releases/tag/v1.5.0) transition. It closes the two-release security rollout opened by 5.0: the bridge gate is removed, per-node Ed25519 request signing and startup node-join authentication become active when configured, and pre-5.0 nodes are refused. The main themes are: 1. [Intra-cluster security](#security). The cryptographic mechanisms staged in 5.0 can now be enabled. Nodes publish verifying keys, protected requests and transport-stream setup are signed, configured startup join credentials are enforced, and the 5.0 version boundary is checked in both join directions. 2. [List-objects scale-out](#list-objects). Listing very large buckets in large clusters no longer falls on the primary gateway. Listings are distributed across all gateways - consistent with the way the AIS datapath has operated since inception. 3. [Shard index v2 and on-demand cache](#shard-index). A new ordered, packed representation removes the decoded per-entry map, substantially reducing allocation and load cost. A new memory-aware cache is aimed primarily at Get-Batch over large TAR datasets, where many member reads repeatedly revisit the same shards. End-to-end cache performance characterization is still pending. 4. [Blob download and prefetch](#blob-downloader). Large remote-object downloads now have explicit size and memory admission rules, parent-to-child cancellation, and cleanup of buffers, manifests, and object locks on failure. 5. Reliability under failure. [Erasure coding](#ec) completes every destination when one of them fails and rebuilds peer streams after node restarts; [global rebalance](#rebalance) continues after per-object failures. 6. [kTLS transmit offload](#ktls) (experimental). An opt-in path, for controlled evaluation, that lets HTTPS GET transfers (i.e., AIS transmit) use sendfile(2) while the kernel - or a capable NIC - encrypts TLS records. Large-scale benchmarks are planned. 7. [Python SDK 2.0](#python), released alongside 5.1. Interrupted `ObjectFile` reads now resume without gaps or duplicate bytes even when the next response starts at byte zero rather than the requested offset. The SDK also improves parallel reads, batch extraction, ETL, and PyTorch integration. The new major version reflects its compatibility changes: the minimum Python version is now 3.10, and several previously announced API removals take effect. Separately, 5.1 sets the objective for [chunked storage](#chunking) - a third storage layout that, like n-way mirroring and erasure coding, is governed by bucket configuration - and deprecates the per-job overrides that contradict it. Implementation is planned for v5.2. > **Upgrade boundary:** v5.0 remains the mandatory bridge from every 4.x release. Upgrade your 4.x cluster to 5.0 before starting 5.1; direct 4.x-to-5.1 upgrades are rejected. See [Upgrade Notes](#upgrade-notes) below for other compatibility changes. --- ## Table of Contents 1. [Security and Upgrade Completion](#security) 2. [List Objects](#list-objects) 3. [S3 Compatibility](#s3) 4. [Object Metadata and Response Headers](#object-metadata) 5. [Shard Index v2 and On-Demand Cache](#shard-index) 6. [Erasure Coding](#ec) 7. [Global Rebalance](#rebalance) 8. [Chunked Storage](#chunking) 9. [Blob Downloader and Prefetch](#blob-downloader) 10. [Internet Downloader](#downloader) 11. [Jobs](#jobs) 12. [Memory Pressure](#memory) 13. [kTLS Transmit Offload (experimental)](#ktls) 14. [Socket Buffers](#socket-buffers) 15. [Native Go API](#go-api) 16. [Python SDK, ETL, and ML](#python) 17. [Miscellaneous Improvements and Fixes](#misc) 18. [Documentation](#documentation) 19. [Removed and Deprecated APIs](#deprecated-apis) 20. [Upgrade Notes](#upgrade-notes) 21. [Acknowledgments](#acknowledgments) --- ## Security and Upgrade Completion v5.0 established the new [network](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/networking.md#v50-network-separation-rule) and metadata boundaries but deliberately suppressed the cryptographic mechanisms while 4.x nodes could still be present in the cluster. v5.1 removes that bridge behavior and completes the transition. ### Per-node request authentication Every 5.1 node generates an Ed25519 keypair at startup and publishes its verifying key through the cluster map. When `auth.intra_cluster.request_auth` is enabled, AIS signs and verifies protected proxy-to-target redirects, node-to-node control requests, and transport-stream connection setup. The signing key remains in memory only. Restarting a node rotates its key; cluster-map propagation distributes the replacement. Transport bundles treat a changed verifying key, network endpoint, or membership state as a new peer incarnation and reopen the affected streams. The setting remains opt-in. With `request_auth` disabled, the arrival-network checks and proxy-mediation rules introduced in 5.0 still apply: when `auth.client_auth_required` is enabled, targets reject unmarked requests sent directly to their public endpoints. An unsigned redirect marker can, however, be supplied by a client and is not authenticated at the receiving target. `auth.client_auth_required` protects requests at proxies; it does not independently authenticate redirected requests at targets. > **Network path and identity:** AIS records each request's [arrival network](https://docs.nvidia.com/aistore/blog/one-cluster-two-three) and enforces the corresponding routing checks even when signing is disabled. This establishes where a request entered, but cannot prove that a public redirect marker came from a gateway. To keep client authentication effective across redirects, enable both `auth.client_auth_required` and `auth.intra_cluster.request_auth` after completing the upgrade. Enabling or disabling `request_auth` requires no cluster or node restart, and no downtime of any kind. Nodes sign immediately when it is enabled and accept unsigned traffic for a bounded convergence window before becoming strict. The same mechanism provides a short startup window while verifying keys converge after a full-cluster restart; it is not intended to make a long-running 5.0/5.1 mixture secure. ### Node-join authentication When `auth.intra_cluster.node_join_secret_path` is configured, 5.1 reads the locally provisioned secret and uses a timestamped HMAC proof to authenticate startup self-join in both directions: - the primary verifies the joining node before admitting its identity and public key; - the joining node verifies the primary before accepting the returned cluster metadata. The secret itself is never transmitted or persisted in AIS metadata. The configured pathname is cluster-wide, while the file must be provisioned locally on every proxy and target with restrictive permissions. Slow keepalive paths that would admit an absent or restarted node use the same proof. The secret is read once during node startup and is not reloaded by a cluster-configuration update. Setting or changing the path persists the new configuration but does not affect running processes until they restart. Administrative-join and force-join authentication remain outside the implemented boundary. See [Node-Join Authentication](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/auth_node_join.md) for the exact status, provisioning order, credential requirements, and recovery procedures. ### Version boundary Joining nodes and primaries exchange their respective AIS software versions. A 5.1 node refuses a pre-5.0 primary, and a 5.1 primary refuses a pre-5.0 node through both self-join and administrative join. Missing version headers are treated as pre-5.0. This closes the two-phase sequence introduced by 5.0: the bridge release accepted 4.x peers long enough to cross the metadata boundary; 5.1 depends on that boundary and fails a skipped-bridge upgrade with a specific compatibility error. ### Additional enforcement Proxy mediation now covers node-control queries as well. Previously, a target would answer requests for its configuration, status, and runtime information sent directly to its public endpoint - even on clusters that require client authentication, which only gateways enforce. Such requests are now rejected, the same way as direct bucket and object requests. Node control goes through a gateway, which authorizes the request before relaying it to the target over the intra-cluster network. Two related changes concern the control plane itself. A control operation now uses one cluster-map snapshot from sender validation through downstream dispatch, so identity decisions within one request cannot straddle map versions. And relayed requests clear system-controlled intra-cluster headers before AIS constructs the next hop. For the complete request matrix and the distinction between proxy mediation and data-plane authentication, see [AuthN: Authentication Boundaries](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/auth_validation.md#authentication-boundaries). ### Object names and append handles Both fixes below originated in reports from outside the project (see [Acknowledgments](#acknowledgments)). [Object names](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/cli/object.md#object-names) are now validated wherever AIS turns them into on-disk paths, not only at the gateway: copy and transform destinations (single- and multi-object), rename, promote, archive destination shards, list- and range-based operations such as prefetch, evict, and delete, names returned by a remote listing, and blob download. Names containing path-traversal components are rejected before they can reach the filesystem. Append handles are bound to the object that created them. A handle carries only a validated tie-breaker for the object's work file; the target derives the work file from the current request's bucket and object, instead of accepting a path encoded for another object. ### Commits - [9e4617f5f](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/9e4617f5f): cross the v5.0 bridge and enable intra-cluster security - [bae0c2a19](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/bae0c2a19): rebuild EC peer streams after restart and membership changes - [2dc9c94b8](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/2dc9c94b8): propagate cluster-map snapshots across control paths - [3e2b18579](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/3e2b18579): require proxy mediation for public target node-control requests - [5b7b51267](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/5b7b51267): cover redirect-marker verification - [5059be970](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/5059be970): remove pre-5.0 compatibility leftovers; reserve feature bit 0 - [96b111f54](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/96b111f54): validate object names wherever they become on-disk paths - [ae2a2716f](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/ae2a2716f): bind append handles to their object --- ## List Objects ### Scale-out across gateways Until now, every [paged listing](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/bucket.md#list-objects) - native or S3 - was forwarded to the primary gateway. Listing very large buckets in large clusters therefore fell squarely on a single node, however many gateways the cluster had. Starting with 5.1, the work of listing large buckets is spread across all gateways (proxies) instead of being concentrated on the primary, consistent with the way the AIS datapath has operated since inception. Each listing is identified by a UUID assigned with its first page; the UUID determines which gateway owns the listing. Any gateway accepts any page and hands it to the owner, so a client - or a load balancer in front of the cluster - can use whichever gateway it likes, page after page. S3 clients need no changes: the listing UUID travels inside the S3 continuation token, which remains opaque (see [S3 Compatibility](#s3)). The primary is still involved in one case: listing a remote bucket that is not yet present in the cluster's bucket metadata. ### Improvements and fixes Targets now report the end of a listing explicitly, rather than leaving the gateway to infer it from page length. A walk error on a target is sticky: it remains visible after traversal finishes instead of disappearing with it. Non-recursive listings, which merge and deduplicate virtual directories across targets, now detect page overflow correctly. Prefix validation and request-error accounting are the same for native and S3 requests. An aborted remote-bucket listing startup, and listing a remote bucket without adding it to bucket metadata, no longer leave ambiguous routing state behind. S3-specific changes - `max-keys`, delimiters, and continuation tokens - are described in [S3 Compatibility](#s3). ### Commits - [79e040dd2](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/79e040dd2): distributed proxy ownership and the new execution flow - [a00f71bec](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/a00f71bec): contextualize proxy-side listing execution - [5dc1c0e79](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/5dc1c0e79): report end-of-listing from targets - [6c5826460](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/6c5826460): merge/dedup overflow and sticky target errors --- ## S3 Compatibility S3 object keys containing `?` now work by default. AIS previously reinterpreted any `?` in the decoded request path as a query delimiter to accommodate TensorFlow clients that embed parameters in encoded object paths. This could address a different key, including on PUT and DELETE. The legacy behavior is available via the opt-in cluster feature `S3-TensorFlow-Query`; enable it only for workloads that require that TensorFlow query format. See [S3 Compatibility: Question marks in object names](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/s3compat.md#question-marks-in-object-names). ### ListObjectsV2 The S3 API now returns exactly one page per request, and `max-keys` is the effective page size. When omitted, it defaults to 1000 or the bucket's maximum page size, whichever is smaller; larger values are capped; `max-keys=0` returns an empty page without listing anything; negative and non-numeric values return `InvalidArgument`. The only supported (nonempty) delimiter is `/`; other values are rejected. Continuation tokens returned by the S3 compatibility API remain opaque. In 5.1, such a token carries the listing UUID (see [List Objects](#list-objects)) together with the underlying marker, which may be an AIS object name or a remote backend's own token. ### Request bodies and errors XML request bodies are now bounded: multi-object delete at 8MiB and bucket versioning at 4KiB, for both declared and streamed lengths. Oversized requests fail with HTTP 413 instead of growing memory without bound. When a gateway fails to relay an S3 object request, the client receives an S3 XML error with status 502 rather than a bare response. ### Commits - [99b821149](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/99b821149): preserve `?` in S3 object keys; opt-in `S3-TensorFlow-Query` - [7782ceec8](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/7782ceec8): honor S3 `max-keys` and paginate list-objects - [7453623b0](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/7453623b0): compound S3 continuation tokens - [087592f05](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/087592f05): bound S3 XML request bodies - [17ded3a05](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/17ded3a05): XML-encode S3 relay failures --- ## Object Metadata and Response Headers Target response headers for GET, PUT, and S3 HEAD are now produced in one place for both the native and S3 APIs, which fixes several differences that S3 clients could see: a streaming cold GET now returns a quoted ETag, as S3 requires; a cold HEAD returns the backend's checksum; and a GET served by the blob downloader carries the remote object's `Last-Modified`. Starting with 5.1, AIS stores a remote S3 object's `Content-Type` with the other supported remote attributes, and returns it as an HTTP header on GET. A cold GET captures the type reported by S3; an S3 PUT into an `ais://` or `s3://` bucket also stores a non-default type. [S3 HEAD](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/s3compat.md#put--get--head) returns it as well, and so does HEAD(object) when the object is present in the cluster. For an object not yet in the cluster, HEAD(object) does not return `Content-Type`. The defaults (`application/octet-stream` and `binary/octet-stream`) are not stored. S3 multipart uploads and the GCP, Azure, and OCI backends are to follow. A HEAD(object) that checks the latest version with a cloud backend can also refresh remote-owned attributes - `Content-Type`, `Last-Modified`, ETag, version, and MD5/CRC32C checksums - when the in-cluster object still matches the remote one but its copy of those attributes is missing or stale. Objects cached before 5.1 can thus pick up their `Content-Type` without being fetched again. The update is best-effort: it is skipped if the object is busy or changes before the write lock is taken. When the in-cluster object does not match the remote, HEAD returns a conflict (HTTP 409) and updates nothing. Local regular and multipart S3 PUTs preserve `x-amz-meta-*` user metadata, and metadata returned by remote S3-compatible backends is propagated as well; AIS-internal keys are excluded from user metadata. ### Commits - [277b4204d](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/277b4204d): consolidate native and S3 response headers - [a5ea27464](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/a5ea27464), [dec516a03](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/dec516a03): store and return Content-Type - [167f25a98](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/167f25a98): refresh remote-owned attributes on HEAD - [88e266f34](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/88e266f34), [4d6b2df4e](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/4d6b2df4e): preserve S3 user metadata --- ## Shard Index v2 and On-Demand Cache Shard indexes accelerate reading archived files - individual files packed inside TAR shards - by mapping file names directly to their offsets and sizes within the shard. v5.1 changes both the persisted representation and the repeated-read behavior while keeping the external GET, Get-Batch, and CLI APIs unchanged. The main expected beneficiary is [Get-Batch](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/get_batch.md) over large sharded datasets, where a request commonly selects only a few members from each TAR while many requests revisit the same shards. ### Version 2 representation Version 1 kept the packed index and also decoded every entry into a `map[string]Entry`. That front-loaded proportional allocation even when a request needed only one member from a large shard. Version 2 stores entries in strict name order and keeps the packed payload plus a `[]uint32` offset table in memory. Lookup binary-searches names in place and decodes offset and size only for the selected entry. Eligible packed and offset buffers use size-classed pools above the page-slab ceiling. The v2 payload fields and uvarint encoding remain the same, but sorted order is now an invariant and the checksum covers the preamble kind as well as the payload. Unit-level measurements documented in [Shard Index](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/shard_index.md#micro-benchmarks) show roughly 2x faster 10K-entry loads and substantially lower steady-state allocation traffic; the primary benefit is avoiding construction of the decoded map. ### On-demand cache The cache is new in 5.1. It is enabled automatically and needs no tuning: it is governed entirely by available memory, growing and shrinking on a best-effort basis and gradually evicting indexes that have not been used for a while. On the first lookup, AIS loads and validates the compact v2 index; simultaneous cold readers share that work. Subsequent reads reuse the loaded index, binary-search the requested file, and read its byte range directly from the TAR. A regular GET of an archived file uses the same path, but Get-Batch is the primary intended consumer. The cache has not yet been benchmarked end to end or run in production. Its benefit depends on shard size, member count, working-set locality, and how often requests revisit the same shards within the retention window. Loaded indexes remain in a per-mountpath cache keyed by object identity and bucket generation: - admission, idle aging, and eviction respond to memory grade; - high pressure stops new admissions and shortens retention; critical pressure clears the cache; - cached references are dropped before returning memory to the operating system; - replacing, removing, rebuilding, or invalidating the source shard removes its cached index. When a target is at high memory pressure, a shard whose index is not already cached is read by sequential archive traversal - the same path as an unindexed shard - rather than by loading the index uncached. This deliberately favors memory stability over lookup latency and can make indexed reads slower than in 5.0 under sustained pressure. Cache activity (misses, loads, denied admissions, evictions, clear-all passes) is logged at verbosity level 4 or with the `cluster` log module enabled (`ais config cluster log.modules cluster`). A growing `deny` count indicates reads falling back to traversal. Index creation is treated as a transaction. AIS revalidates the source before committing the index, and never marks a shard as indexed when its checksum or size no longer matches. Loading distinguishes absent, stale, corrupt, and transient failures; malformed or truncated encodings fall back without panicking. Shard-index metadata follows source-object replacement, local copy, and chunk relocation, without inheriting flags that belong to the old object instance. ### Existing indexes Indexes written by v4.5 through v5.0 have metadata version 1. A 5.1 target classifies an intact v1 index as stale, clears the source marker, and falls back to sequential archive traversal. Object reads continue to work but are not index-accelerated until rebuilt. Rebuild existing indexes without `--skip-verify`: ```console $ ais bucket shard-index build ais://dataset --prefix shards/ --wait ``` See [Shard Index: Upgrading](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/shard_index.md#upgrading) for summary output and rebuild details. We are actively working on on-demand (re)indexing - indexing new writes (PUT, cold GET, copy) into an indexed bucket, and rebuilding v1 indexes, automatically - and plan to include it in the very next release. ### Commits - [33219cda9](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/33219cda9): loading, recovery, persistence, and malformed-input handling - [8c336d790](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/8c336d790): v2 on-disk and in-memory representation - [36206099b](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/36206099b): ownership checks, pooling boundaries, and v1 compatibility - [a659515aa](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/a659515aa): on-demand in-memory cache - [e46d9a80b](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/e46d9a80b): cache eviction and transactional indexing - [fea74ec9b](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/fea74ec9b): shard-index metadata across chunk relocation --- ## Erasure Coding [EC](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/storage_svcs.md#erasure-coding) operates over intra-cluster peer-to-peer streams: to protect an object, a target sends its replicas or slices to multiple peer targets at once. Previously, a failure at one destination terminated the entire send. The remaining destinations were never completed, the error could get lost, and a reader could be accessed after it had been recycled. EC now attempts every destination, reports the first error, and lets go of each reader only after the transport is done with it. EC also keeps its peer streams current. Streams are now rebuilt when a peer target restarts, when cluster membership changes, and when a peer's network endpoint changes - previously, a stale stream could outlive the peer incarnation it was opened for. Encoding is faster and stricter. Data-slice checksums are computed within the same Reed-Solomon encode pass, removing a full scan of the source; for a 512MiB object with 4 data and 2 parity slices, checksum plus encode runs roughly 2x faster. A short data-slice read now fails with `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` even when checksums are disabled. ### Commits - [2fe9ca5f7](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/2fe9ca5f7), [884f31083](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/884f31083), [8ee65f382](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/8ee65f382): complete every destination; reader ownership - [bae0c2a19](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/bae0c2a19): rebuild peer streams across cluster changes - [842b4040f](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/842b4040f), [10db866d0](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/10db866d0): single encode/checksum pass and strict short reads --- ## Global Rebalance A read failure on a single object could previously cut short the traversal of the remaining mountpath, or skip later buckets altogether, while the job still reported completion with zero errors. Rebalance now records the error, counts it (`err-read`), and continues - stopping only when cluster-map placement itself cannot be computed. [Rebalance cleanup](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/rebalance.md#cleanup-mode) now verifies every misplaced source copy through one consolidated path. By default, AIS removes the source only after confirming that the copy on its owner represents the same object. If the peer copy is absent or differs, AIS retains the source; an explicitly forced cleanup may remove a divergent source. ### Commits - [e87fd62ef](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/e87fd62ef): continue rebalance traversal after per-object failures - [1c2dedcbe](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/1c2dedcbe): consolidate per-object cleanup verification --- ## Chunked Storage The objective: chunked objects become the third storage layout, in addition to n-way mirroring and erasure coding, implemented consistently across the entire functionality and configuration - and, like the other two, governed by bucket configuration. A bucket's `chunks` properties are then the single, authoritative statement of how that bucket's objects are stored. Cluster-administrative jobs that operate on many objects converge the data to that configuration, the same way re-mirroring and re-encoding converge it to `mirror` and `ec`, rather than override it. That is the plan for v5.2 (see [Upcoming changes](#chunking-upcoming) below). v5.1 articulates the objective and identifies where current behavior departs from it - most notably rechunk, which can impose its own chunk sizing on a bucket configured otherwise. Single-object operations are a different matter. A client-side multipart PUT, an S3 multipart upload, or a single-object blob download (started explicitly or selected via `api.GetArgs.BlobThreshold`) can choose its own chunk size for that one object. This is a feature - deliberate, advanced usage scoped to a single object. The per-object chunk sizes - including `apc.BlobMsg.ChunkSize`, `--chunk-size` with `ais blob-download` or `ais get --blob-download`, and the blob-downloader default when omitted - remain supported and are not affected by the changes below. Apart from the copy and size-validation fixes below, v5.1 changes no storage behavior. It [deprecates](#deprecated-apis) the per-job rechunk overrides that contradict the objective, and emits warnings where a request depends on them. ### Copy and chunked writes `chunks.max_monolithic_size` is the bucket's hard limit: PUT stores any larger object as chunks, regardless of the rest of the `chunks` configuration. Object copy now follows the same rule. Previously, copying into a bucket with a lower limit - including a copy within the same bucket after the limit was lowered - could leave an oversized object monolithic. Such a copy is now stored as chunks of the destination's `chunks.chunk_size`, including a copy that reads a remote source through the same target. The same change fixes the previous cross-bucket path, which left the source object read-locked after copying it. [ETL transformations](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/etl.md#single-object-transformation) remain an exception when the output size is unknown before the write: AIS cannot use the destination's hard limit to choose a layout in advance. If the transformed size is known, the copy follows the same hard-limit rule. For remote copies, AIS now uses the source object's reported size to decide whether to store the destination as chunks. Multipart-upload parts check the bytes received against their declared size; a copy stored as chunks fails if its source ends before the reported size. AIS closes the source before completing the chunked object and releases it on no-op and error paths as well. A copy that switches from monolithic storage to chunks keeps the source metadata and version; an already-chunked source is not re-chunked solely because it exceeds the hard limit. ### Prefetch: blob-downloader chunking `apc.PrefetchMsg.BlobThreshold` and `apc.PrefetchMsg.BlobChunkSize` are not deprecated, but their semantics change in v5.2. The threshold selects how an object is fetched - a regular cold GET or the parallel blob downloader - and does not itself prescribe how it is stored. With auto-chunking enabled, storage layout follows the bucket's `chunks` configuration regardless of fetch method; the auto-chunking-disabled case below is a deliberate exception. In v5.2: - `BlobThreshold` == 0 disables blob-downloader selection (unchanged; the previous API comment incorrectly described zero as "server default"). - With `BlobThreshold` > 0 and bucket auto-chunking enabled (`chunks.objsize_limit` > 0), blob download applies only at or above max(`BlobThreshold`, `chunks.objsize_limit`) and uses `chunks.chunk_size`; `BlobChunkSize` is ignored, with a log message. - With auto-chunking disabled, blob download applies at or above `BlobThreshold` and uses `BlobChunkSize` (or the blob-downloader default). This is a deliberate exception: `chunks.objsize_limit` == 0 means automatic writes remain monolithic, but reassembling parallel-fetched ranges into a monolithic file degrades performance. Prefetch keeps the chunked result, warns once per job, and suggests `ais bucket rechunk`. For the complete rules - storage layout by object size, and the prefetch mechanism - see [Chunking](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/storage_svcs.md#chunking). ### Upcoming changes Planned for v5.2, implementing the model above: - **Rechunk converges only.** Objects whose layout already conforms to the bucket's `chunks` configuration are skipped rather than rewritten. This includes enforcing `chunks.max_monolithic_size` for existing monolithic objects, which rechunk currently leaves as is. - **Changing `chunks` properties starts rechunk automatically,** as changing `mirror` or `ec` properties already starts re-mirroring or re-encoding. Not to be confused with the [Internet downloader](#downloader), which runs multi-object download jobs. ### Memory and lifecycle Blob download now accounts explicitly for in-flight streaming memory and uses the same effective-free-memory view as the memory manager. Critical pressure rejects all blob downloads; high pressure rejects streaming downloads, while eligible prefetch requests can fall back to ordinary cold GET. The job holds the object's write lock through manifest commit or abort cleanup, stops a streaming download when its client disconnects, propagates parent cancellation into range requests, bounds chunk-read timeouts by `timeout.send_file_time`, honors latest-version policy, and returns synchronous runtime failures when the response has not already been committed. Remote-AIS range requests now retain their contexts across the backend hop. Chunk-size bounds are aligned with bucket `chunks` configuration: a shared 32KiB minimum, up to 5GiB for cache-only downloads, and 64MiB for streaming. Teardown - aborting an uncommitted manifest, releasing the memory claim, unlocking the object, and finishing the job - now runs exactly once on every exit path, including a panic, so a failed download can no longer leave its object write-locked. Buffer ownership between out-of-order chunks and final cleanup is fixed as well, removing a double free. ### Prefetch [Prefetch](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/bucket.md#prefetch-and-evict) is the blob downloader's main background caller: objects at or above `--blob-threshold` are fetched by parallel range reads, smaller ones by regular cold GET. Much of the blob-downloader work in this release is about making that pairing predictable. With `--blob-threshold` set, prefetch no longer checks objects already in-cluster with the backend. Previously, it issued a remote HEAD for every such object - a shortcut to find object sizes - which also implicitly applied the latest-version check. Now the backend is consulted only for objects not in-cluster, and only when their size decides between blob download and cold GET; checking in-cluster objects remains an explicit option (`--latest`). The choice is re-checked once the object is write-locked: if a concurrent GET has brought the object in meanwhile, there is nothing left to download. Prefetch tracks its blob-downloader children from the moment they are scheduled, accounts for each by the object's actual size, and admits them according to current CPU and memory load. Aborting prefetch cancels its in-flight cold GETs and aborts pending blob-downloader children within a bounded time. Once its own work is done, prefetch waits up to 32 minutes for its children, then aborts those still running. Job status now shows how many large objects went through cold GET instead of blob download, and the log says why. A size mismatch between HEAD and GET is logged as a warning. Minimum sizes are now explicit per interface: any non-zero size for the single-object job, `max(--blob-threshold, 1MiB)` for prefetch, and `max(threshold, 128KiB)` for streaming GET. Zero-size objects never go to the blob downloader, and a negative prefetch threshold is rejected. See [Blob Downloader: Size limits](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/blob_downloader.md#size-limits). How prefetch selects chunk sizes in v5.2 is described under [Chunked Storage](#chunking). ### Commits - [94288b635](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/94288b635), [9d59d9c3b](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/9d59d9c3b): blob-download memory admission and accounting - [da7b56436](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/da7b56436): hold object write lock for the blob-download lifecycle - [932f1e36f](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/932f1e36f), [ae2fd7077](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/ae2fd7077): blob-download context propagation and chunk-size bounds - [f98b3ddb4](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/f98b3ddb4), [e882c4f22](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/e882c4f22): exactly-once, panic-safe cleanup; buffer ownership - [44188a16b](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/44188a16b), [1cf61c6c5](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/1cf61c6c5), [8e1ee64fb](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/8e1ee64fb): prefetch selection, accounting, cancellation, and reporting --- ## Internet Downloader The [Internet downloader](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/downloader.md) (`ais download`) runs multi-object jobs that fetch datasets from HTTP(S) sources and remote buckets. > Not to be confused with the [blob downloader](#blob-downloader). The Internet downloader brings in many objects - from arbitrary HTTP(S) sources as well as remote buckets - fetching each one whole. The blob downloader fetches a single large object from a remote bucket, splitting it into concurrent range reads. When the downloader cannot accept another job, the request now fails with HTTP 429, and the job that was never accepted is removed instead of being left behind. Housekeeping retains running and aborting jobs, while rejected and partially constructed jobs release their rate limiter without going through the full cleanup of an accepted job. Removing a job is now serialized with concurrent removals, status, and list requests. ### Commits - [0fa64a616](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/0fa64a616), [15c8822ee](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/15c8822ee), [54915d994](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/54915d994): rejected downloader job lifecycle - [73269b7ba](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/73269b7ba): lock job removal --- ## Jobs In AIS, a [job (also called an xaction)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/cli/job.md#introduction-background-definitions) is an asynchronous operation. Some jobs run across the cluster; others, such as a single-object blob download, run on one target. The changes below concern how jobs are identified and tracked. For multi-object archive, copy, and transform jobs, targets independently derive the same job (xaction) ID without an extra round of coordination. They now use the gateway's two-phase begin timestamp rather than their own clocks, which removes one way they could disagree on the ID: targets processing the same begin a few milliseconds apart, failing the job with `ErrBusy` ("xid mismatch"). The job registry again reports live jobs after its history exceeds the cap; it also gives back excess capacity after bursts. This release continues with consolidation: metadata caching, erasure coding, mountpath walks, space cleanup, LRU, and list-objects all consult the same load advice, and housekeeping intervals scale with memory pressure. AIS continues to use Go's `crypto/tls` for the handshake and receive path, then installs supported transmit keys into the socket. Eligible warm, monolithic object GETs can use `sendfile(2)` while the kernel emits encrypted TLS records. kTLS supports TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 AES-GCM cipher suites. When kTLS cannot be armed because of the kernel, protocol version, cipher suite, or connection state, the connection remains on userspace TLS. AIS serializes the transition and subsequent transmit operations and wipes derived key material after every handshake outcome. "Experimental" refers to mileage, not to the state of the code: every limited benchmark so far has run without failures. What is missing is a large, well-organized benchmark of the right workload on a correctly tuned setup - and possibly Go 1.27, whose `net/http` drives the handshake and application-protocol negotiation (ALPN) on wrapped TLS connections. Both are coming. The capability is off by default and temporarily uses the restart-required `System-Reserved-KTLS` feature bit: ```console $ ais config cluster features System-Reserved-KTLS ``` > Why this name: the bit is deliberately marked system-reserved - a temporary switch for evaluation rather than a stable feature. Once kTLS has enough mileage, we expect to replace it with a regular setting or to enable kTLS by default. Hence, the name, meaning, and polarity may change; do not build deployment automation around it yet. Feature configuration is a complete list: include any other enabled feature names in the same command. It currently applies only to target public listeners. While configured, those listeners use HTTP/1.1 and disable TLS session tickets even for connections that fall back to userspace TLS. We intend to run large-scale kTLS benchmarks soon and publish the results. Throughput and CPU results depend on object size, concurrency, kernel, cipher suite, and whether the kernel performs encryption in software or offloads it to a capable NIC. Early internal measurements point in one direction: the main effect is lower target CPU per transferred byte, and most of it comes from NIC TLS transmit offload; kernel software encryption alone saves comparatively little. When evaluating, measure target CPU per GiB, not throughput alone: once the network is saturated, the gains appear only as lower CPU. Report software kTLS and NIC-offloaded kTLS as distinct configurations, and confirm the NIC path with the NIC's TLS transmit counters. TLS version matters for NIC offload. AIS deliberately has no server-side TLS version setting: targets accept both TLS 1.2 and 1.3 and honor the client's choice, and most clients negotiate 1.3. On many current kernels and NIC drivers, TLS transmit offload is available for TLS 1.2 only; a TLS 1.3 connection armed with kTLS is then encrypted by the kernel in software. See [HTTPS: kTLS transmit offload](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/https.md#ktls-transmit-offload) for host prerequisites, supported paths, fallback behavior, and diagnostics. ### Commits - [9fc6462f2](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/9fc6462f2): initial kTLS TX and HTTPS `sendfile(2)` path - [770c4303e](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/770c4303e): stage-aware unsupported-kernel classification - [a7efcc29c](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/a7efcc29c): key wiping, shutdown serialization, and connection retirement - [7bf39e9a7](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/7bf39e9a7): cache kTLS state in the GET fast path --- ## Socket Buffers AIS storage nodes can now explicitly leave TCP socket-buffer sizing to the operating system. See the [Python changelog](/python/CHANGELOG.md) for the complete API-level list. ### Compatibility changes The minimum supported Python version is now **3.10**; Python 3.8 and 3.9 have reached end-of-life and are no longer tested, and 3.10 through 3.14 are supported. `Object.head()` now uses the selective object HEAD API and returns `ObjectAttributes` rather than a header mapping; the legacy HEAD behavior, the experimental `Object.head_v2()`, and `ObjectAttributesV2` are removed. Dependency minimums move up for upstream security fixes (`requests>=2.33.0`, `urllib3>=2.8.0`) and for Python 3.14 wheels (`xxhash>=3.6.0,<5`). The unused `torchdata` dependency is dropped from the PyTorch extra and pyaisloader; applications that import it directly must install it themselves. ### ObjectFile read resumption An interrupted [`ObjectFile`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/python/examples/sdk/resilient-streaming-object-file.ipynb) read may request the remainder with a byte range, yet receive a complete response starting at byte zero. This occurs for archive members and ETL output, for some range forms, and when a target ignores the range. The reader now tracks the byte position delivered to the application separately from the position consumed in each new response. It detects whether the response actually starts at the requested offset and discards any replayed prefix, so a retry does not duplicate bytes. An uncached remote object also restarts from the beginning rather than attempting a range resume while the object is still being cached. A clean but short response is retried when its expected end is known. ### Parallel reads, retries, and batch results Parallel range GETs validate every response length and stop cleanly after a failure, never releasing shared memory while dispatched work is still in flight. A retried streamed upload rewinds to its starting position, or fails explicitly when it cannot. TAR and ZIP batch extraction reports failed entries as failures rather than as valid empty objects, and preserves both duplicate ZIP names and opaque tracking data. Listing no longer re-copies accumulated entries with every page, and can list buckets across all providers. ### ETL and PyTorch Kubernetes Pod-spec ETL initialization is removed on both server and Python sides. Use [runtime specifications](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/etl.md#runtime-specification) through `Etl.init()` or pure-Python `Etl.init_class()`; persisted legacy ETLs are discarded during upgrade. ETL pipelines also preserve encoded object paths between stages, apply configured connection limits to the active HTTP pool, and reject unsupported chunked PUT framing before transformation. [`AISBatchIterDataset`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/python/aistore/pytorch/README.md) now raises when a batch member reports an error; `cont_on_err=True` logs and skips that member. Reads safely fall back to sequential TAR traversal, but indexed performance returns only after rebuild. After every target reaches 5.1, run the standard build without `--skip-verify` for indexed buckets: ```console $ ais bucket shard-index build ais://dataset --wait ``` Large datasets can be rebuilt by prefix. Use [`ais bucket shard-index summary`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/shard_index.md#summarize-coverage) to monitor valid, stale, invalid, and unindexed shards. On-demand (re)indexing, which will rebuild v1 indexes automatically, is planned for the next release. ### Re-initialize Pod-spec ETLs Pod-spec ETL initialization is removed, and 5.1 discards persisted legacy ETLs. [Initialize them again](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/etl.md#initializing-an-etl) through the runtime-spec API - `Etl.init()` or `Etl.init_class()` in Python. The Python SDK's breaking changes (Python 3.10 minimum, `Object.head()` returning `ObjectAttributes`, removed names) take effect when you upgrade to SDK 2.0.0; see [Python SDK](#python). ### Rechunk overrides are deprecated The rechunk overrides are deprecated in 5.1, with removal planned for 5.2. Move storage policy into bucket `chunks` properties now; see [Removed and Deprecated APIs](#deprecated-apis). ### Experimental kTLS is opt-in No action is required for existing HTTPS deployments. `System-Reserved-KTLS` is disabled by default, requires target restart when changed, and should be enabled only after confirming kernel, TLS-version, cipher, HTTP/1.1, and client reconnect compatibility as described in [HTTPS](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/https.md#ktls-transmit-offload). AIStore **5.0** is a major release. It changes deployment requirements and persisted cluster metadata, replaces the intra-cluster trust model, restructures cluster configuration, and is a mandatory bridge for upgrades - a 4.x cluster must pass through 5.0 on the way to 5.1 and later. > Versions 4.8 and 4.9 were maintenance releases on the 4.7 line. They carried selected fixes from ongoing development rather than successive snapshots of the main branch. Version 5.0 is the next full main-trunk release and contains all development since 4.7, including fixes delivered early in 4.8 and 4.9. The main themes are: 1. [Intra-cluster security](#intra-cluster-security). Through v4.x, the optional intra-cluster authentication path used a shared cluster key and HMAC: one secret held identically by every node, with no way to tell which node signed what. In parallel, AIS permitted a collapsed network configuration in which the public listener and the intra-cluster listeners were the same listener - so a node's only evidence about where a request came from was the request itself. v5.0 requires a distinct public listener, removes the shared-key mechanism, and stages its per-node Ed25519 replacement. Signing remains disabled for the 5.0 bridge and is enabled after the cluster crosses it. 2. [Cluster configuration](#cluster-config). Many sections are now optional in the persisted representation, and sections that contain only defaults are no longer written out in full. This is a metadata-format change, not merely a smaller encoding: it makes operator overrides easier to distinguish, corrects several long-standing zero-value behaviors, and makes persisted 5.0 configuration incompatible with 4.x. 3. [Node lifecycle](#node-lifecycle). Maintenance entry and exit, shutdown, and decommission gain a batch form; administrative membership admission is serialized; rebalance conflicts consistently return `ErrBusy`; and the state a cluster lands in when a maintenance transition does not complete is now named, documented, and retryable. 4. [Control-plane robustness](#control-plane). Heavy job churn, stream cleanup, keepalive work, job startup, and shutdown could interfere with one another in ways that delayed cluster coordination. Those paths are now separated so that activity in one does not stall the rest of the control plane. 5. [Security, reliability, and correctness](#hardening). This release closes a presigned-S3 host-hijacking path, a use-after-free in the memory subsystem, a nil-deref that turned sustained backend throttling into a cluster-wide crash loop, and a concurrency defect that could return one chunk's bytes in place of another's - alongside a systematic pass over object-name, archive, and header validation. Other highlights include ranged [get-batch](#get-batch) reads, opt-in [ETL](#etl) builds with a destination-less `inspect` dry-run, and updates across the CLI, Python SDK, shard index, and Kubernetes deployments. > This release preserves backward compatibility for upgrades from v4.x, including rolling upgrades. > Version 5.0 is, however, the mandatory bridge to v5.1 and later: clusters must upgrade to 5.0 first rather than jump directly from 4.x to 5.1 and later versions. > As always, downgrades are not supported. Optionally, [back up cluster metadata](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/configuration.md#upgrades-and-metadata-backup) and see section [Upgrade Notes](#upgrade-notes) (below) for details. --- ## Table of Contents 1. [Acknowledgments](#acknowledgments) --- ## Intra-Cluster Security For intra-cluster security, 5.0 provides network separation, per-node Ed25519 identity, and node-join authentication. A request is checked first by arrival network and then by sender identity; the second check depends on the first. The network boundary and proxy-mediation policy take effect in 5.0. The cryptographic parts - Ed25519 request signing and node-join proofs - are staged behind the bridge gate for 5.1. ### The three logical networks AIS separates traffic across three logical roles: the **public** network for user-facing API, CLI, SDK, metrics, and external tooling; the **intra-cluster control** network for health, keepalives, cluster metadata, membership, and coordination; and the **intra-cluster data** network for object movement between nodes. These are roles, not necessarily separate physical networks. The data role carries both ordinary target-to-target requests and long-lived data streams; both follow the same network boundary and, after the bridge release, both are authenticated. ### The separation rule Through v4.x, all three roles could collapse onto a single HTTP listener. Starting with 5.0, at least one intra-cluster endpoint is required, and it must be separate from the public endpoint. Intra-control and intra-data may share a listener, with a warning. Public multi-homing remains supported, but each intra-cluster endpoint must use a single IP address or host. Partial configuration - a hostname without its corresponding port - is rejected. ```json "host_net": { "hostname": "ais-pub.example.net", "hostname_intra_control": "ais-intra.example.net", "hostname_intra_data": "ais-intra.example.net", "port": "51081", "port_intra_control": "51081", "port_intra_data": "51081" } ``` The rule is about HTTP endpoint separation, not physical NIC separation. A deployment may use fewer physical networks than logical roles as long as the public listener is distinct. Physical isolation remains strongly recommended for production - bulk data movement fills NIC, TCP, and application queues and causes head-of-line blocking for latency-sensitive control messages - but that is a performance argument, not what this check enforces. A v4.x deployment with a collapsed `host_net` will not start on 5.0. > When the data network is not separately configured, it now defaults to the **control** network. In v4.x it defaulted to **public**, so deployments that omitted intra-data configuration moved object data over the public listener. ### Arrival network Every accepted connection is now identified by the listener that received it: public, intra-control, or intra-data. That identity cannot be supplied or changed by request headers or by a caller-selected address. AIS checks the arrival network before it considers claimed node identity. A public request therefore cannot become an intra-cluster request merely by presenting internal headers. When control and data share a listener, both roles remain available there; the public listener never participates in that fallback. Internal control operations are no longer exposed on the public listener. Daemon and health requests received there expose only user-facing behavior. Public requests that claim an existing node identity are rejected, while self-join requests have any caller-supplied identity removed before processing. Starting with 5.0, these checks are always enforced, regardless of whether request signing or node-join authentication is configured. Network separation does not authenticate the sender. It establishes where a request arrived so that user ACLs and per-node signatures can be applied without trusting caller-controlled headers. > [Blog: One Cluster, Two Perimeters, Three Networks](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/_posts/2026-07-28-one-cluster-two-three.md). ### Per-node identity Under CSK/HMAC every node held the same secret. Any node could produce a signature any other node would accept; a leaked secret compromised the whole cluster with no partial recovery. Verification told a node that *someone in the cluster* had signed, never *which* node - so authorization could not depend on caller identity. The post-bridge Ed25519 model changes both properties. Each node generates its own keypair, and its public key is distributed through the cluster map. A receiver verifies each protected request against the claimed sender's public key, establishing which node sent it. The cluster map therefore gains a per-node verifying-key field. This metadata-schema change is introduced in 5.0, but the bridge leaves the field empty while 4.x nodes may still be present. Starting with 5.1, every admitted node publishes its verifying key and the cluster can rely on it. That implementation is present but not active in v5.0. A 5.0 node generates its keypair locally, strips the verifying key from join metadata, and neither signs nor verifies intra-cluster requests. This keeps a rolling 4.x-to-5.0 upgrade possible. Once the bridge gate is removed, pre-5.0 peers are refused. Keys are held **in memory only**. Every node generates a fresh keypair at startup and, after the bridge, publishes its new public key through the cluster map. There is no signing-key file to provision, protect, back up, or rotate; a restart performs the rotation, and the cluster distributes the replacement key automatically. `rotation_grace` controls transitions when request authentication is changed: signing starts immediately when protection is enabled, strict rejection of unsigned requests begins after the grace window, and nodes continue signing briefly after protection is disabled so the cluster can converge. ```json "auth": { "intra_cluster": { "request_auth": true, "node_join_secret_path": "/etc/ais/join-secret", "nonce_window": "1m", "rotation_grace": "1m", "ttl": "0s" } } ``` `nonce_window` bounds acceptable clock skew for timestamp validation; `ttl` defaults to `0` - signatures do not expire on their own. The entire section can be configured and persisted in 5.0, allowing operators to validate and pre-stage it before upgrading to 5.1. > `intra_cluster` names the protected property rather than the Ed25519 mechanism. The v4.x `auth.cluster_key` spelling is still accepted on load and mapped to the new name. ### What is signed After the bridge, signing covers gateway redirects, target-to-target object and bucket requests, cluster control traffic, machine-learning requests, and long-lived transport streams. Direct user access to an AIS target is now very narrow and specific. GET(object) and PUT(object) and read-only bucket GET and HEAD remain available **iff** both client authentication and intra-cluster request authentication are disabled. Other data operations require proxy mediation or an intra-cluster listener. Redirect markers are accepted only for operations that redirect. These restrictions are enforced in 5.0 and are independent of staged signature verification. The public target listener otherwise exposes read-only daemon status and liveness, readiness, and bootstrap health checks. Internal cluster bookkeeping is restricted to the control listener. ETL management uses the control network, while ETL object I/O uses the data network and remains authorized per transformation. S3 compatibility needed dedicated handling, because presigned S3 requests are redirected and some clients rebuild the redirect URL rather than following it verbatim - discarding any signature attached to the original. AIS now signs redirects issued through the S3-compatible API and preserves the full signed URL in the `Location` header. For clients that reconstruct, there is a cluster feature flag, `S3-Redirect-Rebuild`, which permits unsigned public target S3 requests as a local exception in the target-side S3 API. It is mutually exclusive with the deprecated `S3-Reverse-Proxy` mode, and refuses to coexist with configuration that requires proxy mediation. Long-lived transport streams are authenticated when each connection is opened or re-opened. Authentication covers the stream identity, sender, session, cluster-map version, and a nonce; individual data frames are not signed separately. ### Node-join admission Trust has to start somewhere. A joining node has no cluster-map entry and therefore no public key to verify. Node-join uses a locally provisioned shared secret and HMAC instead. A new `node_join_secret_path` knob specifies the locally provisioned secret for node-join authentication. In 5.0, the path is accepted and persisted, but the secret file is not read and joins are not authenticated. After the bridge release, both initial restart-driven joins require proof of the secret before registration is accepted; missing, empty, or group/other-accessible secret files are rejected. The primary's self-join *response* is authenticated before the joining node accepts cluster metadata. Administrative join and force-join remain future work. Provisioning, rollout, rotation, and recovery procedures are documented in [`docs/auth_node_join.md`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/auth_node_join.md). Separately, cluster-metadata updates and force-join requests now require the current primary proxy/gateway as sender. Previously, a node could apply such updates without first establishing that they came from the primary. ### Startup and the bridge After the bridge, a full cluster restart begins before every node has the latest public keys. During `config.timeout.startup_time`, unsigned control-plane requests are therefore accepted while the cluster map converges. Data-plane requests receive no such exception. v5.0 is a **mandatory bridge release**. It removes CSK/HMAC and permits a mixed 4.x/5.0 cluster while the rolling upgrade completes. The bridge introduces the new cluster-map field without requiring it, allowing every node to cross the metadata boundary before 5.1 begins to depend on per-node verifying keys. Nodes now exchange software versions during join. A 5.0 primary records missing and mismatched versions but remains permissive toward 4.x nodes. Starting with 5.1, both sides enforce the boundary: a pre-5.0 node cannot join a post-bridge primary, and a post-bridge node cannot join through a pre-5.0 primary. An unsupported direct 4.x-to-5.1 upgrade therefore fails with a specific compatibility error rather than a generic join failure. ### See also - [`docs/networking.md`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/networking.md) - network roles, valid and invalid topologies, multi-homing. - [`docs/auth_node_join.md`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/blob/main/docs/auth_node_join.md) - join-secret provisioning, rollout, rotation, recovery. - Blog: [One Cluster, Two Perimeters, Three Networks](https://docs.nvidia.com/aistore/blog/one-cluster-two-three). ### Commits * [32c61952b](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/32c61952b): [security] networking: require pub-net/intra-net separation * [ccdcaa124](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/ccdcaa124): networking: derive request's arrival network from listener identity (part three) * [501112a9d](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/501112a9d): node signing: per-node Ed25519 keys (lifecycle, persistence, cluster map, 5.0 bridge) * [28a85807d](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/28a85807d): Ed25519: remove v4.x CSK/HMAC; Defaults and overrides were difficult to distinguish, and adding a field could rewrite stored configuration across the cluster. In 5.0, many configuration sections become optional in the serialized cluster metadata. Sections that contain only defaults are omitted from persisted and replicated configuration, then restored with the current defaults when loaded. The effective configuration returned by AIS remains complete, while raw persisted configuration is smaller and more clearly represents operator choices. This applies across data movement, listing, rebalance, get-batch, LRU, filesystem health, keepalive, clients, logging, capacity management, transport, checksums, disks, periodic work, downloader, rate limiting, write policies, erasure coding, mirroring, and chunking. ### Behavior changes Making defaults explicit also corrects several zero-value behaviors: * `client_timeout`, `client_long_timeout`, `list_timeout` - zero previously meant no timeout; they now default to 10s, 5m, and 5m. * `transport.burst_buffer` - zero previously resolved to 256 and now resolves to 1024. Other background jobs use a default of 512, doubled for stream bundles when unset. * `space.dont_cleanup_time` - 1h => 30m. * `checksum.type` - at the cluster level, an empty value now denotes an unset section and hydrates to xxhash2. At the *bucket* level an empty value remains a user error. * `write_policy.data` and `.md` - empty hydrates to `immediate`; cluster config now reports the effective policy rather than `""`. * get-batch - `max_wait` 30s => 20s, `warmup_workers` 2 => -1 (disabled), realigning defaults with production. Also, `keepalivetracker.retry_factor` is deprecated while preserving its 5.0 behavior, and keepalive intervals are now checked against `timeout.max_keepalive`. Transient updates can no longer change settings that require full cluster validation, and `rebalance` and `fshc` sections in an initial plain-text configuration must be specified completely rather than partially. ### New and renamed settings * `lso` - a new list-objects section replaces hardcoded buffering and timeouts with settings for local walks, remote pages, listing idleness, and post-listing quiescence. * `net.http.backend_idle_conn_time` - separates the backend/cloud idle-connection timeout from `net.http.idle_conn_time`, which remains bounded for intra-cluster clients. The backend setting has no upper bound; zero now selects the system default for both settings instead of unlimited idle time. * `net.http.pub` - an optional, all-or-nothing TLS override for the public listener (see [TLS](#tls)). * `auth.enabled` => `auth.client_auth_required`; `auth.cluster_key` => `auth.intra_cluster`; `auth.cluster_key.enabled` => `auth.intra_cluster.request_auth`. Previously each was single-node, so taking down a rack meant issuing separate requests, each triggering its own rebalance decision with no coordination between them. ```console $ ais cluster add-remove-nodes start-maintenance ``` The API retains the existing single-node field and adds a list of node IDs. Completed transitions are idempotent: nodes already active, fully in maintenance, or removed are skipped; a batch that changes nothing does not create a new cluster-map version or start a rebalance; and a node that disappears during finalization no longer aborts the remaining batch. ### Serialized admission The primary now admits one administrative membership change or administrator-initiated rebalance at a time. Overlapping changes are rejected while a rebalance is running, eliminating races in which two operations made decisions against different views of the cluster. Automatic self-join is the documented exception. Rebalance conflicts now consistently return `ErrBusy`. The same underlying condition previously surfaced as several different errors depending on which path detected it, which made it hard for callers - and for the CLI - to distinguish "retry this" from "this failed". ### Incomplete transition An interrupted maintenance entry or exit now leaves the node in a documented **incomplete transition** state. Previously this state had no name or recovery procedure. One cause is a rebalance listener being aborted when another target leaves the cluster. Recovery starts by retrying the administrative operation. Mixed batches may contain both active and maintenance nodes, and the cluster warns when a required rebalance was skipped. ### Maintenance mechanics Stopping maintenance now probes nodes in parallel, retries only the failed subset, skips nodes that are already active, and rejects nodes being decommissioned. A cluster change and rebalance are started only when at least one target actually transitions. Get-from-neighbors is enabled before reactivation begins and handed over to the rebalance when one is needed, keeping reads available throughout the transition. ### Node version on join Nodes now advertise their software version when joining, and the primary tracks nodes that differ from its own version. During the 5.0 bridge, a missing version identifies a pre-5.0 peer but does not prevent the rolling upgrade. Starting with 5.1, a missing or invalid version is rejected: 4.x nodes cannot join a post-bridge 5.x cluster, and post-bridge nodes cannot join through a 4.x primary. A lightweight API can query the software version of an individual node. ### Commits * [68445ca01](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/68445ca01): [API change]: batch (decommission, start-maintenance, shutdown)-node * [5412f88e3](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/5412f88e3): node lifecycle: batch cleanup; parallel stop-maintenance health checks (part four) * [1f021d3ec](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/1f021d3ec): node lifecycle: early GFN for stop-maintenance; batch regression test * [6b948f503](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/6b948f503): node lifecycle: serialize administrative membership admission (part seven) * [b383ee073](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/b383ee073): node lifecycle: clarify text and comments, with minor ref (part twelve) * [81497a2df](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/81497a2df): advertise node version on join; primary to track --- ## Control-Plane Robustness This release addresses a set of independently reported problems with one shared root cause: latency-sensitive coordination work was riding on paths that could be blocked by bulk activity. ### Scheduling and stream cleanup Heavy job churn could fill an internal work queue and stall a target's control plane - the failure mode behind [#336](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/issues/336), observed during sustained S3 LIST activity. Scheduling now absorbs bursts without blocking callers, runs all work that is due, and prevents invalid intervals from causing busy loops. Transport-stream cleanup received the same treatment. Bursts of stream additions and removals no longer block producers, temporary queue growth is reclaimed, and pending changes are drained before streams stop during node shutdown. ### Concurrent job startup Starting one background job no longer blocks the registration or renewal of unrelated jobs. The change preserves list-objects startup throttling, while duplicate transport registrations for multi-object copy and archive jobs now fail immediately instead of contending later. ### Off the keepalive path Shared data-mover activity is no longer tied to fast keepalives. Nodes track active and recently used streams locally, addressing [#316](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/issues/316), where keepalive and health timeouts could cause spurious target evictions. Keepalive failures are now reported as warnings in node-state alerts. Erasure-coding stream cleanup is likewise independent of keepalive. Streams close only after a full minute with no active or recent work, and stream open/close operations are serialized. Required streams now open before an erasure-coded bucket is created, not only when existing bucket properties change. ### Termination signals SIGINT, SIGTERM, and SIGQUIT now reach the main daemon directly, so hundreds of active jobs cannot delay or block shutdown. Legacy SIGHUP/SIGUSR1 handling was removed. ### Rebalance and list-objects A newer rebalance can now preempt an older one without stale state leaking across generations. Late-stage or abort notifications retain the ID of the rebalance that produced them, preventing asynchronous cleanup from being attributed to a newer job ([#317](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/issues/317)). List-objects also fixes a broadcast deadlock at large cluster sizes. The previous 128-request fanout limit could block the designated target while other targets waited for its remote page; LIST broadcasts now reach all targets concurrently. The fix was verified with a 300-target remote listing test. ### Commits * [3c1cb6e3a](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/3c1cb6e3a): housekeeper: eliminate channel-full stall; refactor and micro-optimize * [cf2252cbf](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/cf2252cbf): transport stream collector (gc): eliminate channel-full; remove unused min-heap * [6a641c75e](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/6a641c75e): xreg: move xaction startup outside renewal lock (fix) * [fd864653a](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/fd864653a): remove shared-DM from keep-alive piggy-back; expire locally * [100a036ea](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/100a036ea): SIGTERM, et al.: remove from housekeeper; rewire via the main rungroup * [ac0c10d74](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/ac0c10d74): list-objects: prevent deadlock with one-batch R-flow broadcast --- ## Security, Reliability, and Correctness Several of the problems in this section were reported to us privately; see [Acknowledgments](#acknowledgments). ### Presigned S3 host hijacking SigV4 regions were concatenated into upstream URL authorities, which allowed crafted credentials to redirect requests to attacker-controlled hosts. S3 URLs are now constructed from the configured remote bucket, and the signed region is required to match the bucket's backend region. Regression coverage proves host-hijacking requests are rejected before reaching the attacker endpoint. ### Multipart upload buffer lifetime During a multipart upload, the HTTP client may continue reading a request body after a redirect or retry has returned control to AIS. The upload buffer could previously be recycled while that read was still in progress, causing a panic or silent data corruption. Buffers now remain owned until all outstanding reads finish. ### Backend throttling crash loop An OCI 429 response could trigger a nil dereference while AIS formatted the error. Under sustained backend throttling, restarted targets would immediately encounter the same response and crash again, turning throttling into a cluster-wide crash loop. 429 responses now preserve the original error and remain safe to report and retry. ### Multipart download concurrency A multipart download worker could reuse a buffer slot before the earlier chunk had filled it, returning a later chunk's bytes in the earlier chunk's position. Slots are now reserved before work starts. Errors and stream closure cancel outstanding range requests, caller HTTP settings are preserved, and every returned range is checked for its exact expected length. ### Object-name and path validation Gateways validate object names before redirecting a request, but a directly reached target could not assume that validation had happened. Targets now validate object names independently for GET, PUT, HEAD, DELETE, and PATCH, as well as S3 object operations, copy sources and destinations, and multi-object delete. Object names, virtual-directory prefixes, and archive paths are rejected when they could escape an AIS mountpath. ### Custom metadata validation Custom metadata is now validated at every identified ingress and persistence boundary. Reserved symbols and oversized metadata are rejected in API updates, remote-backend response headers, multipart-upload initialization, and LOM xattr packing. ### Bounds, overflow, and egress * Oversized `aws-chunked` lengths can no longer wrap during conversion and panic a target; they are rejected against S3's 50,000 GiB object limit before allocation. * Malformed extended-object headers are rejected when any declared length exceeds the available payload. * TAR and ZIP entries with empty names are rejected instead of reaching an out-of-bounds access. * Downloader and dSort SSRF protection now recognizes IPv4 destinations embedded in NAT64, 6to4, and Teredo addresses, including carrier-grade NAT and local-use ranges. * dSort external key-map URLs can no longer reach loopback, private, link-local, unspecified, or multicast destinations. * CLI archive extraction is confined to the selected destination and rejects parent traversal. * Empty target-side `/s3` paths are rejected instead of reaching an object operation without a bucket name. ### Access-control fixes Promote sources are now restricted to absolute paths beneath `/var/lib/ais/promote`. The same range semantics apply regardless of which target serves the data. Three forms are supported per entry: * `Start=0, Length=0` - the whole object. * `Length > 0` - a fixed-length range. * `Length = -1` - open-ended, reads from `Start` to EOF. A non-zero `Start` with `Length = 0` is rejected; use `-1` to read to the end. `Start < 0` or `Length < -1` are invalid, and `Start >= size` returns HTTP 416 (range not satisfiable). > Note: a range over a `.tar` or similar shard is a raw range over the archive object itself, not over an entry within it. To range within an entry, set `archpath`. The Python SDK carries the same semantics: `Batch.add()` accepts and validates `start` and `length` for both objects and archive members. Documentation includes curl and Python examples for all three forms. ### Zero-size entries Zero-byte objects and archive members are now supported throughout get-batch and streaming paths. Readers are closed correctly even when there is no payload. ### Authorization All input buckets in a batch request are now authorized independently, rather than relying on the permissions of the first bucket. ### Commits * [576bbf86e](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/576bbf86e): get-batch: support ranged reads for objects (chunked or mono) and archived files * [5e4010d80](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/5e4010d80): get-batch: support open-ended read ranges (length=-1 reads to end) * [c61dd1ac9](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/c61dd1ac9): get-batch: handle zero-size remote objects * [b366558e9](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/b366558e9): get-batch: handle zero-size archived files (part two) * [4d0a8a6b8](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore/commit/4d0a8a6b8): get-batch: authorize all input buckets (part two) --- ## AuthN and Access Control ### Token revocation `DELETE /v1/tokens` is now authorized rather than open, and revoked tokens are validated upstream. Client-supplied revoked-list versions are ignored. AuthN rejects requests carrying revoked tokens, and the CLI confirms before revoking. `ais auth rm token` silently ignored its positional argument - the token was only ever read from `-f`/`--file`, `$AIS_AUTHN_TOKEN_FILE`, or the default token file, despite the help text advertising `TOKEN | TOKEN_FILE`. It now reads the positional as a literal token; a file is still accepted via `-f`, and a bare invocation falls back to the environment variable and then the default file. ### Token validation All tokens now require an expiration and a supported signing method. JWTs with non-zero Base64URL padding bits are rejected. Unavailable signing keys are distinguished from invalid tokens, so an operational problem no longer looks like an authentication failure. ### Roles and ACLs Invalid empty ACL entries are discarded when roles are added, updated, or read. Permissions for the same cluster or bucket are merged rather than duplicated, and role changes are reflected immediately for affected users. The CLI's `whoami` command reports the same effective permissions that AuthN enforces. ### Keys and operations AuthN preserves its existing RSA key sizes and PEM formats while adding coverage for externally provisioned keys. When it is absent, the public listener continues to use the TLS settings in `net.http`; the existing on-disk format is otherwise unchanged. Upload IDs, part numbers, and ETL arguments are decoded once and interpreted the same way on gateways and targets. A 206 response is sent only after the correct range position has been established. GET error reporting now distinguishes failures that happen before any response bytes are sent from expected disconnects after transmission begins. Archive close and flush failures are propagated, local I/O warnings are less noisy and more accurate, and missing object metadata is distinguished from a missing file. ### Custom metadata An S3 backend HEAD request no longer mutates cached object metadata. Eviction also detaches cached custom metadata, closing a race between prefetch and cold GET.
